parts.text:
6
In still air, a bird can fly at a speed of 10 m s–1. The wind is blowing from the east at 8.0 m s–1.
In which direction must the bird fly in order to travel to a destination that is due north of the bird’s
current location?
A
37° east of north
B
37° west of north
C
53° east of north
D
53° west of north

hints: Notice wind blowing from the east means the air velocity is $8.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ toward the west, so the bird is being pushed west.
To stay on a due north track, the bird's own $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ velocity must provide an $8.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ component toward the east to cancel that drift.
Draw the velocity triangle with hypotenuse $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and opposite side $8.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, then use $\sin \theta = 8.0/10$ with $\theta$ measured east of north.
walkthrough: Wind from the east blows toward the west at $8.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, so without correction the bird would drift west of north.
Let $\theta$ be the angle of the bird's heading east of north. Its velocity relative to the air has magnitude $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
For the ground track to be due north, the east-west components must sum to zero: $10 \sin \theta - 8.0 = 0$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, with east taken as positive.
The bird must therefore aim into the wind, $53^{\circ}$ toward the east from north. This is option C.

A.explanation: 37 degrees east of north would give an east component of only $10 \sin 37^{\circ} \approx 6.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, which is too small to cancel the $8.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ westward drift.

B.explanation: Heading west of north adds a west component to a wind already pushing west, so the resultant cannot stay on a due north track.

C.explanation: An eastward component of $10 \sin 53^{\circ} \approx 8.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ exactly cancels the westward wind, leaving a resultant velocity due north.

D.explanation: 53 degrees west of north points into the wind direction and gives a large resultant westward component, so the bird would drift west of due north.
